chunks: "Heat matters for three reasons. First, it's generated inside the cell any time current flows, mainly I squared R in the internal resistance.
A 2 amp-hour cell at 5C is 10 amps through maybe 50 milliohms, so 5 watts inside a small package. If that can't escape, the cell warms up. Second, heat accelerates ageing.

Side reactions that grow the SEI layer, consume lithium and degrade the electrolyte all speed up roughly exponentially with temperature, and a common rule of thumb is that degradation rates roughly double for every 10 degrees, though the exact figure varies.
So a pack that lives at 45 degrees ages much faster than one at 25. Third, and most important for safety, there's thermal runaway.
Above roughly 80 to 130 degrees C the decomposition reactions inside the cell become exothermic, so heat makes more heat.
If the heat generation outpaces cooling, it's a positive feedback loop: the cell vents, burns, and can set its neighbours off.

So we put limits on it: charge only between about 0 and 45 degrees, discharge within about minus 20 to 60, NTC sensors that the charger and BMS watch, derating at high temperature, and thermal design: spacing, heat spreading, airflow, and barriers between cells."
